newsitem.title: HAITI: Haiti still searching for new prime minister.
newsitem.headline: Haiti still searching for new prime minister.

text.p: Nearly three weeks after Prime Minister Rosny Smarth resigned, Haitian President Rene Preval has not named a successor to the unhappy job of carrying out a controversial economic reform plan.

Smarth, who resigned under fire from anti-privatisation groups, and his cabinet have continued work while waiting for a new team. Preval has made no public statements about the departure of Smarth or his possible replacement.

"They have not found the lucky winner," said a former politician whose name has been suggested in political circles as a possible candidate. He said his past experience with the dicey politics of privatising state enterprises had made him happy to stay out of the debate.

Both former President Jean-Bertrand Aristide, who still enjoys wide popular support, and a grassroots political group that led sometimes violent demonstrations against Smarth have said privatisation would devastate the impoverished country.

The government's economic plan calls for nine state-run enterprises including the electricity and phone companies to receive private investment through joint ventures, management contracts and concessions. Preval has said the plan is the best way to attract capital and technology without outright sale of state enterprises.

"There is no other way," said the potential candidate for prime minister, who asked not to be identified. "If someone would suggest how to go left, I would go left, but I haven't heard anyone suggest how to do that."
Both detractors and supporters criticised Smarth for not communicating details of the economic plan well enough for the people to understand it or to trust the government.

"The ability of any government to get the widespread support of the population for such a plan is to be clear about what the programme entails," Philippe Nouvel, head of the Caribbean Division at the World Bank, said.
Legislators in Haiti's Chamber of Deputies, who nearly ousted Smarth with a no-confidence vote in March, judged him severely on the communication issue.
"This government has been the least communicative ever," said Deputy Alix Fils-Aime, who has also been named as a possible replacement for Smarth and has said he would be willing to take on the post.
"Who would make a good prime minister? I would," he said.

Other names suggested include former Prime Minister Smarck Michel, who resigned during Aristide's presidency out of frustration with Aristide's apparent lack of will to carry out the reforms, and Preval adviser Leslie Voltaire.
